title: Rikki-Tikki-Tavi

teacherSummary.text: A young mongoose, washed from his burrow by a flood, is adopted by an English family in a bungalow in India. He befriends Darzee the tailorbird and learns of the cobras Nag and Nagaina. He kills the snake Karait, then Nag in the bathroom, and destroys Nagaina's eggs. Nagaina threatens the boy Teddy; Rikki lures her away, follows her into her hole and kills her.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Rikki-Tikki-Tavi,” how does Kipling show courage in defense of home? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Rikki-Tikki-Tavi, how does Kipling develop the idea of courage in defense of home? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Rikki-Tikki-Tavi develops the idea of courage in defense of home. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and conflict shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Rikki-Tikki-Tavi (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of courage in defense of home. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Rikki-Tikki-Tavi suggests about courage in defense of home. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's characterization and conflict), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Rudyard Kipling uses characterization in Rikki-Tikki-Tavi to complicate the reader's understanding of courage in defense of home. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Rikki-Tikki-Tavi within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of courage in defense of home responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Rikki-Tikki-Tavi alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of courage in defense of home follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Rikki-Tikki-Tavi and its treatment of courage in defense of home. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's characterization and conflict, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Rikki-Tikki-Tavi as evidence for a larger claim about courage in defense of home in Rikki-Tikki-Tavi. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Rikki-Tikki-Tavi as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of courage in defense of home. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Rikki-Tikki-Tavi.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Rikki's curiosity makes him a hero. Useful evidence: “Run and find out” (Rikki-Tikki-Tavi, paragraph 20): His nature. On characterization: Rikki is curious, brave and loyal; Nagaina is cunning; Darzee is foolish but loyal. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Animal violence; colonial setting. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail.
contentNotes.studentPreview: Heads-up: this story includes animal violence; colonial setting.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Why does the writer include this, and what does it make us notice?”
